title.en: Distinguish commanded, estimated and true pose

summary: Keep the commanded motion, the estimate from sensors and the simulated ground truth as separate quantities and show which is drawn.
objective: Make a robot navigation scene honest about what the robot knows versus what is true.
applies_when: A mobile robot or vehicle moves and reports its position.
Odometry, dead reckoning or localisation is part of the subject.
A path is drawn from the robot own estimate.
intent_signals: the map does not line up
example_prompts: Show the commanded path and the odometry estimate side by side.
Demonstrate why wheel odometry drifts over time.
negative_signals: Scenes where the robot pose is simply authored and no estimation is claimed.
Fully localised systems where the estimate is the subject of a different treatment.
not_for: Scenes where the robot pose is simply authored and no estimation is claimed.
Fully localised systems where the estimate is the subject of a different treatment.

principles: Three different quantities are routinely drawn with the same arrow: what was commanded, what the robot estimates, and where it actually is. Conflating them removes the entire subject of estimation.

Odometry is computed from wheel feedback, and a controller can also be configured to compute it from the commanded values instead. Which one drifts more depends on the error model: with ideal actuation and correct geometry both agree exactly, command-based estimation ignores slip and actuation error, and noisy or miscalibrated feedback can be the worse of the two. The documentation establishes the authority of each source, not a ranking of their errors.

Parameter errors show up as systematic distortions rather than noise: an incorrect wheel separation makes curves wrong, and an incorrect wheel radius makes the robot move faster or slower than expected.

Drift accumulates under a declared error model: slip, wheel-radius error, quantisation or noise. State that model, because without one there is nothing to expect and nothing to check, and a demonstration then needs enough travel and turning for the modelled error to become visible.
implementation: Draw only the poses you actually have. Commanded and estimated poses are always available; a true pose exists only in simulation or from an independent reference such as a motion capture system or a survey, and must not be manufactured from the same estimate.
State whether odometry uses feedback or commanded values, since the two behave differently.
Expose the geometric parameters, such as wheel separation and radius, and let the viewer perturb them to see the characteristic error signature.
Show the accumulated error over the run rather than only the instantaneous difference.

Where a correction such as a landmark or map update exists, show what it actually does: a filter usually adjusts the estimate incrementally with a covariance, while a hard reset to a known pose is a different, stronger operation. Say which one the scene implements.
observable_checks: Drive a closed loop and compare the closure error against the declared error model: with the ideal model the estimate closes and that is correct, while with slip or a radius error it should fail to close by roughly the predicted amount. A true path that fails to close points at the controller or the plant, not at the estimator.
Perturb the wheel separation and confirm the error appears in curves rather than as random noise.

Switch between feedback and commanded odometry and confirm the difference matches the modelled error source: identical results under ideal actuation, and a divergence that grows with the modelled slip or miscalibration.
Confirm every drawn path is labelled with which pose it represents.

creative_affordances: Presentation of uncertainty, from a growing ellipse to a fading trail, is a free design choice.
A deliberately exaggerated drift makes the lesson visible in a short run when the exaggeration is stated.
known_limits: Authored guidance citing one controller documentation for odometry sources and parameter effects; it does not model wheel slip or sensor noise characteristics.
No robot or simulation has been run for this record.

claims.statement: A differential drive controller computes odometry from hardware feedback, and when configured for open-loop operation it computes odometry from the commanded values instead; an incorrect wheel separation parameter makes the robot behave incorrectly in curves and an incorrect wheel radius makes it move faster or slower than expected.
claims.scope: Documented behaviour of one differential-drive controller implementation; it does not quantify drift for any specific robot.

source_refs.locator: Odometry from feedback; open_loop parameter; wheel_separation and wheel_radius descriptions
